title: Skin: Your Body's Shield
summary: How skin protects the body, keeps it at the right temperature, senses touch, and heals itself after a small cut.
poll: Skin does more jobs for the body than most people realize.

versions.title: Skin Protects You
versions.text:
Skin covers your whole body. It is your biggest part. It has a big job to do.

Skin is a shield. It keeps germs and dirt out. It keeps water in. Without skin, your body could not stay safe.

Skin also lets you touch and feel things. It feels a soft pat. It feels a hot cup. It feels a sharp pin. It sends a message to your brain fast.

Skin helps you stay just right, not too hot and not too cold. When you are hot, skin makes sweat. The sweat cools you down. When you are cold, skin helps keep heat in.

Sometimes skin gets a small cut. Do not worry. Skin can heal itself. A scab forms over the cut. New skin grows under it. Soon the scab falls off.

Take care of your skin. Wash it. Keep it dry when you can. Then your shield can do its job well.

versions.title: Skin: Your Body's Shield
versions.text:
Skin covers your whole body. It is the biggest part of your body. It has many jobs to do.

Skin acts like a shield. It keeps out germs and dirt. It also keeps water inside your body. Without skin, your body would not stay safe or well.

Skin also lets you touch and sense the world around you. It feels a soft pat, a hot cup, or a sharp pin. Tiny parts in the skin send a message to your brain very fast.

Skin helps keep your body at just the right heat, not too hot and not too cold. When you get hot, your skin makes sweat. As the sweat dries, it cools your body down. When you get cold, your skin helps hold heat close to you.

Sometimes skin gets a small cut. There is no need to worry. Skin can heal itself over time. A scab forms over the cut to protect it. New skin cells grow underneath. After a while, the scab falls off on its own.

Take good care of your skin by washing it and keeping it dry when you can. Then your shield can keep doing its job well.

versions.title: Skin: Your Body's Shield
versions.text:
Skin covers your whole body, and it is actually your biggest organ. It does several jobs at once. Each job helps keep you safe and well.

Skin works like a shield for your body. It blocks most germs and dirt from getting inside. It also keeps water from leaving too fast. Without skin, your body would have a hard time staying safe. Skin also lets you touch and sense things around you. It can feel a soft pat, a hot cup, or a sharp pin. Tiny parts in the skin send that feeling to your brain fast.

Skin also helps keep your body at just the right heat. When you get hot, your skin makes sweat. As the sweat dries, it cools you down. When you get cold, your skin helps hold warmth in. This keeps your body safe in different kinds of weather.

Skin can also heal itself after a small cut. First, a scab quickly forms over the cut. The scab protects the cut from new germs. Under the scab, new skin cells slowly grow. These new cells fill in the hurt spot. After a while, the scab falls off on its own. Then your skin looks and works like before.

A new cut may feel sore for a little while. That soreness usually fades after a day or two. It is a normal part of healing.

Taking care of your skin helps it do all these jobs well. Wash it and keep it reasonably dry. Then your body's shield can keep protecting you every day.

versions.title: Skin: Your Body's Shield
versions.text:
Skin covers your whole body, and it is actually the biggest organ you have, even bigger than your heart. It does several jobs at once. Each job helps keep your whole body safe and well.

Skin works like a tough shield for your body. It blocks most germs and dirt from getting inside, and it keeps water from leaving too fast. Without skin, your body would have a hard time staying safe and healthy for long. Skin also lets you touch and sense the world around you. Tiny parts inside the skin pick up a soft pat, a hot cup, or a sharp pin. They send that feeling racing to your brain very fast.

Skin also helps keep your whole body at just the right heat, not too hot and not too cold. When you get too warm, your skin makes sweat. As the sweat slowly dries on your skin, it carries heat away and cools you down. When you get too cold, your skin helps hold warmth close to your body instead of losing it.

Skin also has its own way of healing after a small cut. A scab quickly forms over the cut to keep out new germs. Under the scab, fresh skin cells slowly grow, almost like rebuilding a tiny wall. After a while, the scab falls off on its own, and the skin underneath looks healed.

A new cut may feel a little sore for a while. That soreness usually fades within a day or two. It is simply a normal part of healing.

Taking good care of your skin, by washing it and keeping it reasonably dry, helps it keep doing all these jobs well. Then your body's shield stays strong. It can keep protecting you every single day.

versions.title: Skin: Your Body's Shield
versions.text:
Skin covers your whole body. It is the largest organ you have, bigger than your heart or your lungs. It does several jobs at once, all day and all night. Each job matters in its own way.

First, skin acts like a shield. It blocks most germs and dirt from getting inside your body. It also keeps water from leaving too fast, which keeps your body properly hydrated. Without this shield, your body would have a hard time staying healthy.

Second, skin senses the world around you through tiny parts called receptors. They can feel a soft pat, a hot cup, or a sharp pin. They send a signal racing along nerves to your brain, faster than you can blink.

Third, skin helps regulate your body's temperature. When you get too warm, sweat glands make sweat. The sweat evaporates off your skin and cools you down. When you get too cold, blood vessels in your skin constrict, which helps keep warmth close to your body.

Finally, skin can heal itself after a small cut. A scab quickly forms to protect the spot from new germs. New skin cells slowly grow underneath it until the cut closes up completely.

Taking good care of your skin, by washing it regularly and keeping it reasonably moisturized, helps it keep doing all of these jobs well.

versions.text:
Skin covers your whole body, and it is the largest organ you possess, larger than your heart, lungs, or any other organ. It does several jobs at once, around the clock, without ever taking a break.

First, skin acts as a shield. It blocks most germs, dirt, and harmful things from entering your body, and it also keeps water from leaving too fast, which helps your body stay properly hydrated. Without this shield, your body would struggle to stay healthy.

Second, skin senses the world around you through tiny parts called receptors. They can feel a soft pat, a hot cup, or a sharp pin, and they send a signal racing along nerves to your brain, usually faster than you can blink.

Taking good care of your skin, by washing it regularly, protecting it from the sun, and keeping it reasonably moisturized, helps it keep performing all of these jobs well.

versions.title: Skin: Your Body's Shield
versions.text:
Skin covers your whole body and is the largest organ you possess, considerably larger than your heart, lungs, or any other internal organ. It does several jobs at once, around the clock, without ever pausing.

First, skin acts as a shield made of layers, including an outer epidermis and a thicker dermis beneath it. Together these layers block most germs, dirt, and harmful things from entering your body, and they also keep water from leaving too fast, which helps your body stay hydrated.

Second, skin senses the world around you. Tiny parts called receptors, found throughout the dermis, pick up pressure, temperature, and pain with real precision. When something touches you, these receptors send a signal racing along nerves to your brain.

Third, skin helps regulate your body's temperature through a physiological process using sweat glands and blood vessels. When you get too warm, sweat glands within the dermis release sweat onto the epidermis, and as it evaporates, it cools you down. When you get too cold, blood vessels inside the dermis constrict, which helps keep warmth near your body's core.

Scientists have studied skin's layers for centuries. In the 1600s, an Italian scientist named Marcello Malpighi used an early microscope to examine a layer deep inside the epidermis, later named the Malpighian layer in his honor. His drawings helped others understand that skin is built from several separate layers.

Finally, skin has a remarkable ability to heal itself after a minor cut. A clot forms, and a scab develops over the cut, protecting the area from new germs while fresh skin cells regenerate underneath, layer by layer, until the wound closes completely.

Caring for your skin, by washing it regularly, protecting it from strong sun, and keeping it moisturized, helps it keep performing all of these jobs well, year after year.

Caring for your skin, by washing it regularly, protecting it from strong sun, and keeping it reasonably moisturized, helps this remarkable organ continue performing all of its vital functions well, year after year.

Skin covers your entire body and is, in fact, the largest organ you possess, considerably larger than your heart, lungs, or any other single internal organ you have; it performs several essential functions simultaneously, around the clock, without ever pausing for even a moment throughout your entire life.

First, skin functions as a protective shield composed of distinct, specialized layers, including an outer epidermis and a considerably thicker dermis situated beneath it. Together these layers block the overwhelming majority of germs, dirt, and harmful substances from entering the body, while also preventing water from escaping too rapidly, which helps the entire body remain properly hydrated at all times. Without this layered barrier, the body would struggle considerably to remain safe and healthy for any extended period of time.

Second, skin constantly senses the surrounding environment through an extraordinarily dense network of specialized nerve cells. Tiny structures called receptors, distributed throughout the dermis, detect pressure, temperature, and pain with remarkable precision and speed. The instant something touches you, whether a soft pat, a hot cup, or a sharp pin, these receptors transmit a signal racing along nerves to your brain, typically faster than you can even consciously blink.

Third, skin helps regulate your body's internal temperature with great precision, keeping it neither too hot nor too cold regardless of the surrounding weather conditions outside. When you become overheated, sweat glands within the dermis release sweat onto the epidermis, and as this sweat evaporates from the skin's surface, it carries heat away and cools your body down considerably. When you become too cold, blood vessels inside the dermis constrict noticeably, a physiological process that helps conserve warmth near the body's core instead of losing it uselessly to the surrounding air.

Scientists have studied skin's intricate layered structure for several centuries, but one especially influential map of it was drawn by an Italian anatomist named Marcello Malpighi during the 1600s. Using an early, fairly primitive microscope, he carefully described a distinct layer deep within the epidermis, which scientists later named the Malpighian layer in his honor, a name still used in anatomy today. His meticulous drawings helped later generations of researchers understand that skin is built from several separate, cooperating layers, each with its own specific function to perform within the whole.

Finally, skin possesses a remarkable capacity to heal itself after a minor injury of almost any kind imaginable. Within minutes, a clot forms and a protective scab develops over a cut, shielding the area from new germs while blood vessels and specialized cells work actively beneath the surface to rebuild what was damaged. Fresh skin cells gradually regenerate underneath, layer by layer, until the wound has closed completely and the scab eventually falls away entirely on its own, revealing healed tissue beneath.

Caring for your skin, by washing it regularly, protecting it carefully from strong sun, and keeping it reasonably moisturized, helps this remarkable organ continue performing all of its many vital functions well, year after year, for an entire lifetime of use.

MID.modelAnswer: Skin helps regulate body temperature in two opposite ways. When a person becomes too hot, sweat glands in the skin release sweat, and as the sweat evaporates, it carries heat away and cools the body down. When a person becomes too cold, blood vessels inside the skin constrict, which helps conserve warmth near the body's core instead of losing it to the air. Because of these two responses, skin helps keep the body at just the right temperature no matter what the weather is like outside.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the layered structure of skin, including the epidermis and dermis, allows it to perform several different jobs at once. Support your answer with evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained the roles of the epidermis and dermis.

HIGH.modelAnswer: The layered structure of skin allows it to perform several different jobs at once because each layer contributes something specific to the whole. The outer epidermis, together with the dermis beneath it, blocks germs and dirt from entering the body while also preventing water from escaping too quickly, which keeps the body hydrated. At the same time, the dermis contains receptors that detect pressure, temperature, and pain, as well as sweat glands and blood vessels that help regulate body temperature by releasing sweat or constricting to conserve warmth. This layered design, first mapped in detail by Marcello Malpighi in the 1600s, shows that skin is not a single simple covering but a coordinated organ whose separate layers each perform a specific, necessary function.
